topic: Tự dựng IP-KVM cho Homelab với espkvm: Cứu hộ và quản lý server từ BIOS qua trình duyệt trên ESP32-P4 thay thế PiKVM

repos.name: espkvm
repos.description: IP-KVM on the ESP32-P4: HDMI capture, USB keyboard and mouse, and a browser console over HTTPS

repos.name: PiKVM
repos.description: Open and inexpensive DIY IP-KVM based on Raspberry Pi

notes.audience: Các lập trình viên, sysadmin và dân chơi homelab tại Việt Nam đang tìm giải pháp điều khiển, cứu hộ máy chủ từ xa cấp độ BIOS với chi phí thấp thay cho PiKVM.
notes.angle: Tự chế IP-KVM cứu hộ server từ BIOS bằng vi điều khiển ESP32-P4 và mạch chuyển HDMI-to-CSI: không cần Raspberry Pi, không cần cài OS Linux, flash thẳng từ trình duyệt với độ trễ chỉ 60ms.

facts.fact: espkvm chạy trên vi điều khiển ESP32-P4 kết hợp với chip cầu chuyển đổi HDMI-to-CSI Toshiba TC358743 để đưa màn hình, chuột, phím lên trình duyệt qua HTTPS.
facts.quote: This one is built from an ESP32-P4 and a Toshiba TC358743 HDMI-to-CSI bridge, and costs a fraction of a commercial KVM-over-IP.

facts.fact: Thiết bị hoạt động ngoài hệ điều hành mục tiêu, cho phép can thiệp vào BIOS, menu khởi động hoặc máy chưa cài OS.
facts.quote: So it still works where remote desktop cannot: a BIOS screen, a boot menu, a kernel that will not come up, a machine with no operating system on it at all.

facts.fact: Firmware có thể flash trực tiếp vào ESP32-P4 từ trình duyệt máy tính (Chrome hoặc Edge) qua Web Serial mà không cần cài đặt toolchain.
facts.quote: Connect the board over USB and install the firmware from this page. No toolchain, no download, nothing uploaded anywhere

facts.fact: Giao thức web console hoàn toàn độc lập, gói gọn trong một file nén khoảng 70 KB được nhúng sẵn trong firmware mà không tải tài nguyên bên ngoài.
facts.quote: The console is one gzipped file of about 70 KB, with nothing fetched from outside.

facts.fact: Độ trễ phản hồi từ khi di chuột đến khi thấy chuyển động trên màn hình là khoảng 60 ms trên chip ESP32-P4 bản revision 3.x.
facts.quote: From moving the mouse to seeing it: about 60 ms on rev 3.x.

facts.fact: Định dạng MJPEG ở độ phân giải 1080p đạt khoảng 20 fps trên mọi phiên bản chip ESP32-P4.
facts.quote: At 1080p, MJPEG runs at about 20 fps on any board; H.264 at 25-27 fps on rev 3.x and about 7 on rev 1.x.

facts.fact: Trên bo mạch Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH, cổng USB OTG nối với máy mục tiêu nằm ở chân cắm MX1.25 chứ không phải cổng USB-C.
facts.quote: The USB 2.0 OTG that goes to the target is on the MX1.25 connector, so the lead is MX1.25 to USB-A.

facts.fact: Đường dây USB OTG cấp nguồn ngược 5V từ máy mục tiêu về bo mạch, nếu rút cáp ở phía máy tính sẽ làm KVM khởi động lại.
facts.quote: The target's 5 V comes back down that lead: pulling it at the target's end restarts the KVM.

facts.fact: Trình duyệt bắt buộc phải tin tưởng chứng chỉ CA tải từ thiết bị thì các tính năng bàn phím, chuột và chuẩn nén H.264 mới hoạt động.
facts.quote: The picture works without it, but the keyboard, the mouse and H.264 need a page the browser trusts.

facts.fact: Không được đưa espkvm trực tiếp ra Internet vì secure boot và mã hóa flash bị tắt, đồng thời bản nâng cấp firmware chưa được ký số.
facts.quote: Secure boot and flash encryption are off, and update images are not signed.

facts.fact: Hỗ trợ tính năng Virtual Media cho phép giả lập ổ đĩa boot máy tính từ file ISO/img lưu trên thẻ microSD hoặc flash nội bộ.
facts.quote: Virtual media: boot the target from an image | works; from microSD or the device's flash

facts.fact: Để điều khiển bật/tắt nguồn và nút reset vật lý của máy tính chủ, espkvm yêu cầu nối thêm optocoupler (cách ly quang) hoặc relay.
facts.quote: Power, reset and Wake-on-LAN, the power and disk lights | works; power needs an optocoupler or a relay

facts.fact: Nút BOOT trên bo mạch Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH bị chia sẻ với chân Ethernet nên chip chỉ đọc trạng thái nút này một lần ngay khi bắt đầu khởi động.
facts.quote: The BOOT button (GPIO 35) is also an Ethernet pin, so the device reads it once, early in start-up. For the password reset: press reset, release, then hold BOOT.

facts.fact: PiKVM DIY phiên bản dựa trên Raspberry Pi tốn từ $30 đến $100 tùy cấu hình phần cứng.
facts.quote: Costs between $30 and $100 depending on the features desired. Even the most expensive configuration will be cheaper than a $500 commercial IP-KVM.

facts.fact: PiKVM đạt độ trễ video H.264 từ 35 đến 50 mili-giây nhưng phải chạy cả hệ điều hành nhúng Arch Linux ARM trên thẻ nhớ SD.
facts.quote: ~35-50 milliseconds of video latency. This is the smallest delay of all existing solutions.

install: cd web && npm ci && npm run build && cd ..
caveats: Không đưa thiết bị trực tiếp ra Internet công cộng vì chưa hỗ trợ Secure Boot, chưa mã hóa flash (flash encryption off) và file firmware cập nhật không được ký số (unsigned images).
Trên bo mạch Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH, cổng Type-C chỉ dùng để flash nạp firmware và xem serial log (chip CH343); kết nối phím chuột tới máy target bắt buộc dùng jack nối MX1.25 sang USB-A.
Nguồn 5V từ máy tính mục tiêu chạy ngược vào chân USB OTG, việc rút cáp ở phía máy tính mục tiêu sẽ làm ngắt nguồn và reboot KVM.
Bàn phím, chuột và luồng stream H.264 sẽ không hoạt động trên trình duyệt nếu chưa tải và cài đặt tin cậy chứng chỉ CA nội bộ của espkvm (cert.pem).

Bo mạch Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH được bán lẫn lộn giữa bản chip rev 1.x (H.264 chỉ được 5-7 fps ở 1080p) và rev 3.x (25-27 fps), mã sản phẩm của hãng không ghi rõ phiên bản mà phải xem ký tự đuôi của chip (có chữ X là rev 3.x).

Cáp camera FPC nối mạch HDMI CSI: nếu dùng Geekworm C790 thì cắm thẳng cáp 22-pin đi kèm, nhưng nếu dùng mạch Waveshare HDMI-to-CSI 15-pin thì phải mua thêm cáp chuyển 15-sang-22-pin (loại dành cho Raspberry Pi 5).
Chức năng bật nguồn và reset ATX không cắm trực tiếp được mà phải tự nối thêm rơ-le hoặc mạch optocoupler bảo vệ.
gaps: Tổng chi phí mua linh kiện lẻ (bo mạch ESP32-P4, mạch HDMI-to-CSI C790, cáp MX1.25) tại các sàn TMĐT Việt Nam là bao nhiêu so với chi phí mua PiKVM hoặc combo Raspberry Pi 4?
Nơi đặt mua cáp chuyển đổi MX1.25 sang USB-A ở Việt Nam hoặc sơ đồ bấm chân jack MX1.25 cụ thể?
Tốc độ nạp và gắn (mount) file ISO thực tế qua giao thức Virtual Media từ thẻ microSD vào BIOS có nhanh bằng USB thật hay không?
Độ ổn định khi cắm chạy liên tục 24/7 trong tủ mạng gia đình (nhiệt độ chip P4 khi mã hóa phần cứng liên tục) có cần thêm quạt tản nhiệt không?

## espkvm/espkvm (https://github.com/espkvm/espkvm)
Description: IP-KVM on the ESP32-P4: HDMI capture, USB keyboard and mouse, and a browser console over HTTPS
Homepage: https://espkvm.io
Language: C; license: Apache-2.0; created 2026-07-22; last push 2026-11-13
Latest release: v.0.83.1 (2026-11-13)
README (start):
# ESP-KVM

  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  

Like remote desktop, except it does not run on the machine. A small board plugs
into that machine's HDMI output and a USB port, and serves its screen, keyboard
and mouse to a browser. So it still works where remote desktop cannot: a BIOS
screen, a boot menu, a kernel that will not come up, a machine with no operating
system on it at all.

That is an IP-KVM. This one is built from an ESP32-P4 and a Toshiba TC358743
HDMI-to-CSI bridge, and costs a fraction of a commercial KVM-over-IP.

New to the idea? [What an IP-KVM is, and why you might want one](https://espkvm.io/blog/what-an-ip-kvm-is/)
— what remote desktop cannot do, and where people actually use this.

  Flash a board from the browser →
   · 
  Try the console
   · 
  Quick start

  
   
  

**From whatever you have to hand.** The console is a web page, so the machine
you drive the target from can be a laptop, a phone or a tablet - nothing to
install on either end. Touch gets a trackpad and an on-screen keyboard rather
than a shrunken desktop, the page can be installed from the browser to run
full-screen like an app, and where the link is too thin for video the screen
comes through as text.

> **Built on [jrowny/p4kvm](https://github.com/jrowny/p4kvm).** The hard part -
> bringing up the TC358743 and getting frames out of the ESP32-P4's CSI
> receiver - was solved there first, and this project would not exist without
> it. See [Credits](#credits).

## Status

Useful for what it does today, and honest about the rest.

| | |
|---|---|
| Video: follows the target's resolution, MJPEG and H.264 | works; H.264 needs HTTPS |
| Keyboard, mouse, media keys, pasting text in a layout | works |
| From a phone or a tablet | works; touch trackpad, pointer stick, pinch zoom and on-screen keyboard |
| Several viewers, one in control | works; plus a view-only sign-in for others |
| Virtual media: boot the target from an image | works; from microSD or the device's flash |
| Recording, screenshots, dashcam, timelapse | works; on a microSD card |
| Reading a text screen as text, watching it for words | works; text modes only |
| Macros, runbooks, a scheduler | works |
| A command palette (Ctrl+K), your own buttons on the bar | new; the palette also finds every setting by name |
| Notifications to Telegram, ntfy, a webhook or the browser, with a screenshot | works |
| Power, reset and Wake-on-LAN, the power and disk lights | works; power needs an optocoupler or a relay |
| HDMI-CEC remote | works; on TC358743 boards |
| A gamepad for a console | works on a Switch |
| Device profiles: pointer, gamepad and video settings for each target | new, the device picks one from HDMI-CEC or the USB guess |
| Screen areas: react when a part of the screen changes, stops changing, matches a saved picture or turns a colour | new |
| The target's serial console, and its log over the network | works |
| ESP-KVM Tools on the target: its name and addresses, the clipboard both ways, a clean shutdown | new; needs [ESP-KVM Tools](https://github.com/espkvm/tools) on the target |
| HTTPS, your own certificate, Let's Encrypt over Tailscale | works |
| Login, two-factor sign-in, reset by a button | works |
| Wi-Fi with up to three known networks, a setup hotspot, Ethernet with Wi-Fi as the backup | works; on boards with a Wi-Fi chip |
| Tailscale or WireGuard | works; off by default |
| Home Assistant over MQTT | works; off by default |
| Updates over the network, with rollback and a trial for remote devices | works |
| A small status display, a battery-backed clock | works; optional |
| HDMI audio, in the console and in recordings | new; on TC358743 boards, three wires to the P4 |
| Sound over USB: the device as a USB speaker for the target | new; for boards without HDMI audio, such as the JetKVM Mini |

Every row in detail: [docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md](docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md#what-works-in-detail).

What is coming next is in the [roadmap](ROADMAP.md).

  

The device in Home Assistant — every value reported live over MQTT, discovered automatically.

**Do not put this on the public internet.** It has a login, two-factor sign-in
and TLS, and has had a security review of my own but not an external one. Secure
boot and flash encryption are off, and update images are not signed. Keep it on
a network you trust, or reach it over the Tailscale or WireGuard built into it
([docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md#reaching-it-from-outside-tailscale-or-wireguard)).

## Hardware

An ESP32-P4 board does the work, a TC358743 capture board turns the target's
HDMI into a stream the P4 can read, and a camera ribbon joins the two. That is
all it takes; an optocoupler for the power button and a small status screen
are optional.

**The capture board:** a [Geekworm C790](https://wiki.geekworm.com/C790) or a
[Waveshare HDMI to CSI Adapter](https://www.waveshare.com/wiki/HDMI_to_CSI_Adapter).
The M5Stack Unit PoE-P4 takes its own [Add-on Display In](https://shop.m5stack.com/products/add-on-display-in-for-poe-p4-lt6911d) instead.

**The ESP32-P4 board**, one of these:

| Board | Network | Chip revision | |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-ETH](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-eth/) | Ethernet | 1.x or 3.x | tested; the default |
| [Espressif ESP32-P4 Function EV](https://espkvm.io/boards/funcev/) | Ethernet, Wi-Fi | 1.x or 3.x | tested |
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-NANO](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-nano/) | Ethernet, Wi-Fi | 1.x or 3.x | tested |
| [Guition ESP32-P4-M3-Dev](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-guition/) | Ethernet, Wi-Fi | 1.x or 3.x | tested |
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-WIFI6-POE-ETH](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-poe/) | Ethernet with PoE, Wi-Fi | 1.x or 3.x | tested |
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-WIFI6](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-wifi6/) | Wi-Fi only | 1.x or 3.x | tested |
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-WIFI6-DEV-KIT](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-wifi6-devkit/) | Ethernet with PoE, Wi-Fi | 1.x or 3.x | tested |
| [DFRobot FireBeetle 2 ESP32-P4](https://espkvm.io/boards/firebeetle2-p4/) | Wi-Fi only | 1.x | tested |
| [M5Stack Unit PoE-P4](https://espkvm.io/boards/m5-poe-p4/) | Ethernet with PoE | 1.x | tested |
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-NANO-WIFI6-DB](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-nano-wifi6-db/) | Ethernet, 5 GHz Wi-Fi | 3.x | tested |
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-Module-DEV-KIT](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-module-devkit/) | Ethernet, Wi-Fi | 1.x or 3.x | tested |
| [Espressif ESP32-P4X-C5-Function-EV](https://espkvm.io/boards/funcev-c5/) | Ethernet, 5 GHz Wi-Fi | 3.x | untested |
| [Waveshare ESP32-P4-WIFI6-DB](https://espkvm.io/boards/p4-wifi6-db/) | 5 GHz Wi-Fi only | 3.x | tested |
| [VIEWE ESP32-P4-Pi](https://espkvm.io/boards/viewe-p4-pi/) | Ethernet, Wi-Fi | 1.x | untested |
| [M5Stack Unit PoE-P4X](https://espkvm.io/boards/m5-poe-p4x/) | Ethernet with PoE | 3.x | untested |

"Untested" means the image is built from the vendor's schematic and nobody has
run it yet; if you have one, say how it went. Another P4 board? [Every ESP32-P4
board I have looked at](https://espkvm.io/boards/all/) says whether it can work. Rev 3.x silicon runs H.264 three
times faster at 1080p, and it takes its own image: the boot log prints the
revision, and so does the chip, **ESP32-P4NRW32X** with an X being rev 3.x.

To choose between them: [compare the boards](https://espkvm.io/boards/compare/).
Photos, cables, which port goes to the target, cases and status screens are in
[docs/BOARDS.md](docs/BOARDS.md), with what rules a board out if yours is not
listed.

## Quick start

1. **Flash it.** From the browser, in Chrome or Edge:
   [espkvm.io/flash](https://espkvm.io/flash/). Or take your board's
   `espkvm---merged.bin` from the
   [releases](https://github.com/espkvm/espkvm/releases) and write it at 0x0:

   ```sh
   esptool --chip esp32p4 -b 921600 write-flash 0x0 espkvm---merged.bin
   ```

   Drivers and serial-port notes: [docs/FLASHING.md](docs/FLASHING.md).
2. **Connect it:** the network, HDMI from the target, and the board's USB OTG
   port to the target. Which port that is depends on the board - on the
   P4-ETH it is the MX1.25 header, not the USB-C ([cables](docs/BOARDS.md#cables)).
3. **Open https://espkvm.local/** and sign in as **admin / admin**; it asks for a
   new password first. A board with Wi-Fi and no cable opens a hotspot,
   **ESP-KVM-xxxx**, with the console at `http://192.168.4.1/`.
4. **Trust the device's CA** (Settings → Security → Download CA
   certificate, or `http://espkvm.local/cert.pem`) as a trusted authority. The
   picture works without it, but the keyboard, the mouse and H.264 need a page
   the browser trusts.

Certificates of your own, Let's Encrypt over Tailscale, IPv6, the hotspot and
updates: [docs/SETUP.md](docs/SETUP.md).

## If it does not work

The usual causes - the USB lead in the wrong port, an untrusted certificate, a
target that looks for a monitor too early, a reboot to explain - and how to tell
them apart are in [docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md). Still
stuck: [Discussions](https://github.com/orgs/espkvm/discussions), with the board,
the capture board and the log from Diagnostics.

## Building from source

The web console lives in a submodule ([espkvm/console](https://github.com/espkvm/console)),
so clone with `--recursive` (or run `git submodule update --init` in an existing
clone). Without git, take `espkvm--source.tar.gz` from a release (from
0.56.3 on): GitHub's own "Source code" archives leave the submodules out.

```sh
git clone --recursive https://github.com/espkvm/espkvm
tools/install-idf.sh                          # ESP-IDF 6.1, once
. tools/env.sh
cd web && npm ci && npm run build && cd ..    # the console is embedded in the firmware
idf.py build
idf.py -p /dev/ttyACM0 -b 921600 flash
```

There is no `menuconfig` step for the default board: everything it needs is in
`sdkconfig.defaults`. To build for another board, apply its overlay - see
[boards/](boards/README.md).

The console can also be developed against a simulated device, with no hardware
attached at all:

```sh
cd web && npm run dev:mock
```

### Tests

```sh
tools/test.sh          # all of it: the host C and the console, in seconds
tools/test.sh host     # just the C
tools/test.sh web      # just the console
```

## How it works

The P4's hardware JPEG and H.264 encoders compress the picture, and one USB
port presents a keyboard, two pointers and a disk to the target. At 1080p,
MJPEG runs at about 20 fps on any board; H.264 at 25-27 fps on rev 3.x and
about 7 on rev 1.x. From moving the mouse to seeing it: about 60 ms on rev 3.x. The console is one gzipped file of about 70 KB, with nothing
fetched from outside.

Video, input, recording, virtual media, reading the screen, security and
updates, in detail: [docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md](docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md).

## API

Everything the console does is available over HTTP: settings, video and the
screen as text, recording, virtual media, power, HDMI-CEC, the target's serial
console, and, behind a switch in Settings → Security, the keyboard and
pointer. The full list, how to sign in, and the WebSocket protocol are in
[docs/API.md](docs/API.md).

To hand it to an AI agent there is a skill,
[espkvm/skills](https://github.com/espkvm/skills), and an MCP server,
[espkvm/mcp](https://github.com/espkvm/mcp).

### Built by other people

- **[guacamole-espkvm](https://github.com/Crisspii/guacamole-espkvm)** by
  [Crisspii](https://github.com/Crisspii) - an Apache Guacamole protocol plugin,
  so several devices sit in one Guacamole as ordinary connections, with the
  credentials held on the server. It speaks this device's own protocol rather
  than wrapping a browser: H.264 and MJPEG, keyboard, pointer and virtual media.
  Experimental, v0.1.0, tested against Guacamole 1.6.0.

## Repository layout

```
components/
  tc358743/       HDMI bridge driver, EDID profiles
  video_pipeline/ CSI capture, MJPEG and H.264 codecs, published frame store
  kvm_hid/        composite USB H

README (start):
# Open and inexpensive DIY IP-KVM based on Raspberry Pi
[](https://discord.gg/bpmXfz5) [](https://www.reddit.com/r/pikvm)

A very simple and fully functional Raspberry Pi-based KVM (Keyboard-Video-Mouse) over IP that you can make with your own hands. This device helps to manage servers or workstations remotely, regardless of the health of the operating system or whether one is installed. You can fix any problem, configure the BIOS, and even reinstall the OS using the virtual CD/DVD or Flash Drive.

The website: [pikvm.org](https://pikvm.org). Also check out [the documentation](https://docs.pikvm.org) and join the [Discord Community Chat](https://discord.gg/bpmXfz5) for news, questions and support! Also you can visit our [Support Forum](https://forum.pishop.com/c/pikvm).

| Web UI                                     |
| ------------------------------------------ |
|  |

# Features
* Can be made based on **Raspberry Pi 2**, **Pi 3**, **Pi 4**, **Pi 5** and **Zero2W**;
* **FullHD video** using advanced **HDMI-to-CSI bridge** or **USB dongle**;
* [Proven](https://docs.pikvm.org/latency) lowest **35-50ms H.264 latency** among all KVMs on the market;
* WebRTC, H.264-over-HTTP and MJPEG video;
* Bootable **Virtual CD/DVD** and **Flash Drive**, ability to store images on **NFS**;
* USB **Keyboard** and **mouse** (with leds and the wheel), Bluetooth HID, Mouse jiggler, full support of PS/2;
* **Control the server power** using ATX functions;
* Access via **Web UI** or **VNC**;
* Ability to use **IPMI BMC**, **IPMI SoL**, **Redfish** and **Wake-on-LAN** to control the server;
* **The ready-made OS** with read-only filesystem;
* **Extensible authorization** and HTTPS out of the box;
* **Health monitoring** of the Pi;
* Control **GPIO** ports and **USB relays**;
* 100% Open Source!

# Variants

PiKVM supports several different hardware configurations, referred to as **platforms**.
All of them uses our common open source software stack.

### PiKVM V3 & V4 - Now with web camera!

* **PiKVM V4** and **V3** are our own **plug-and-play, fully assembled, industrial grade, robust** devices.
    Supports **H.264 video, audio, microphone and web camera** transmission, **host power management**, **mass-storage emulation** and much more.
    They are really well-made, reliable things which you can use yourself or provide to your clients.
    V4 and V3 also have more features than DIY builds.

* **PiKVM V2** and **V1** devices are **DIY** so you can make it with your own hands.
   If you don't know where to put your old Raspberry Pi, here's a great goal.

## Fully-featured and modern IP-KVM
* **Cheaper, but better than commercial solutions**  
  Costs between $30 and $100 depending on the features desired. Even the most expensive configuration will be cheaper than a $500 commercial IP-KVM.
* **Easy to build - For the V1 variant**  
  A ready-to-use OS that can be created just by running `make build` and installed to an SD-card using `make install`. The hardware can be made in half an hour and without soldering.
* **The widest hardware support**  
  There are many ways to build a PiKVM. Video capture devices can be attached using the CSI-2 or USB interfaces. Raspberry Pi models 2, 3, 4 or Zero2W may be used. Any combination of hardware is supported, and PiKVM implements the maximum possible set of features.
* **Very low latency**  
  ~35-50 milliseconds of video latency. This is the smallest delay of all existing solutions.
* **Extra lightweight and fancy Web UI**  
  No weird proprietary clients. No ugly Java applets. Just use your favorite browser to connect to the PiKVM. No flash plugins either!
* **Keyboard and mouse**  
  Mouse usage works directly in the browser. The keyboard emulator supports displaying the state of the keyboard LEDs.
* **Mass Storage Drive**  
  On the Raspberry Pi 4, 5 and Zero2W, PiKVM can emulate a virtual CD/DVD or Flash Drive. A live image can be uploaded to boot the attached server.
* **ATX power management**  
  With a very simple circuit that can be assembled on a breadboard, the power button of the attached server can be controlled using the ATX button headers on the motherboard.
* **Security**  
  PiKVM can be opened to the Internet and no one will get access without the password. SSL is used to protect traffic from being intercepted by third parties.
* **Local monitoring**  
  PiKVM monitors the health of the Raspberry Pi board and will warn you if it's too hot or is not receiving enough power.
* **GPIO management**
  You can control GPIO and USB relays via the web interface. The extensible interface allows you to make anything out of it.

## Production-ready  
* **Linux-based embedded OS**  
  The PiKVM OS is based on [Arch Linux ARM](https://archlinuxarm.org) and can be customized for any needs. Thousands of pre-built binary packages are at your service and can be updated with a single command!
* **Read-only filesystem**  
  By default the OS runs in read-only mode, as an embedded system should. This prevents damage to the memory card due to a sudden power outage.
* **VNC server**  
  The managed server and its BIOS can be accessed using a regular VNC client which supports JPEG compression.
* **IPMI BMC and Redfish**  
  Use `ipmitool`, `ipmiutil` or any existing network infrastructure that supports IPMI to monitor and manage the server's power. Redfish and `redfishtool` supported too.
* **Wake-on-LAN**  
  PiKVM can be configured to power up a managed server using WoL. This will be available in the Web menu.
* **Extensible authorization methods**  
  Multiple PiKVMs can be configured to use a [common authorization service](https://github.com/pikvm/kvmd-auth-server). PAM and its rich authorization mechanisms can also be used to integrate PiKVM into your existing authentication infrastructure.
* **Macro scripts**  
  If repetitive actions must be performed on the attached server (or on several different servers), a macro can be recorded with keyboard & mouse actions and can be played back multiple times.

## 🌟 What is NanoKVM?

NanoKVM is a series of compact, open-source IP-KVM devices based on the LicheeRV Nano (RISC-V). It lets you remotely access and control computers as if you were sitting in front of them, making it useful for servers, embedded systems, and other headless machines.

## 📦 Product Family

Choose the NanoKVM model that best fits your deployment:

- **NanoKVM-Cube Lite:** A barebones kit for DIY users and bulk deployments.
- **NanoKVM-Cube Full:** A ready-to-use kit with a case, accessories, and a pre-flashed system SD card.
- **NanoKVM-PCIe:** A PCIe-bracket form factor for internal chassis mounting. It draws power from the PCIe slot and supports optional Wi-Fi and PoE.
- **[NanoKVM-Pro](https://github.com/sipeed/NanoKVM-Pro):** A higher-performance version with major upgrades:
  - **Resolution:** Up to **4K@30fps / 2K@60fps**.
  - **Network:** **1Gbps Ethernet + PoE + Wi-Fi 6**, upgraded from 100Mbps Ethernet.
  - **Latency:** Hardware-accelerated encoding reduces latency from 100-150ms to **50-100ms**.

  

> If you are looking for a USB-based KVM solution, check out [NanoKVM-USB](https://github.com/sipeed/NanoKVM-USB).

The board ESP-KVM was written on, and the default image: the flasher offers it first. Ethernet only, no Wi-Fi.

Wiring
The USB-C port is the flashing and console bridge (CH343), not the target's port.
The USB 2.0 OTG that goes to the target is on the MX1.25 connector, so the lead is MX1.25 to USB-A.
The target's 5 V comes back down that lead: pulling it at the target's end restarts the KVM.
The camera connector is the narrow 22-pin one. The C790 has a 22-pin connector on its back and a 22-pin ribbon in the box, so they join directly. A capture board with only the wide 15-pin connector, like Waveshare's adapter, needs a 15-to-22-pin ribbon (sold as a Raspberry Pi 5 camera cable).
Measured

MJPEG at quality 70, rev 1.3 chip:

Mode	fps	Bitrate
1920x1080	20	17.5 Mbit/s
1280x720	45.5	16.8 Mbit/s
1024x768	56	17.6 Mbit/s

A still screen costs nothing, since unchanged frames are skipped. H.264 on this chip runs at 5-7 fps at 1080p and 17 fps at 720p, but an idle desktop costs 170 kbit/s against MJPEG's 8.5 Mbit/s: it is for narrow links, not for smoothness. A rev 3.x chip does 25-27 fps at 1080p.

Good to know
The BOOT button (GPIO 35) is also an Ethernet pin, so the device reads it once, early in start-up. For the password reset: press reset, release, then hold BOOT.
The microSD writes at 40 MHz because the slot's power comes from the chip's LDO 4.
Waveshare sells it with either revision, and the product code does not tell which. The boot log prints chip revision:.

Another ESP32-P4 board with Ethernet and the same camera connector can run it too. The pins are set in menuconfig, not in the code.

What to expect
Connect the board to this computer with a USB-C cable.
Press Install and pick the board’s serial port from the list the browser shows. On Linux it is usually /dev/ttyACM0, on Windows a COM port.
Wait about a minute. The whole flash is written — bootloader, partition table and firmware — so this also works on a board that has never run anything.
Plug in Ethernet and open https://espkvm.local/. Accept the certificate warning, sign in as admin / admin, and set a password.
Optional: turn on Settings → System → Offer firmware updates. It is off by default. With it on, the console tells you when a newer build is out and installs it in one click — your browser checks, the device itself never goes online. You will not need this cable again unless something goes badly wrong.
Two USB ports, one of them right. These boards have a USB-serial port and a USB-OTG port. Flashing goes through the serial one — the OTG port is what the target machine sees as a keyboard. If the port list is empty, try the other socket.
If Install fails to connect (“Failed to initialize”), hold the board’s BOOT button, press and release RESET, then let go of BOOT, and press Install again. That puts the chip in its bootloader when the automatic reset does not take. Also close anything else using the port: another tab with the serial monitor, Arduino IDE or a terminal.
If it still fails, ask in GitHub Discussions. Write the board name and the error text from the dialog.
If your board is already running ESP-KVM, you do not need this page or a cable. In the console, Settings → System either checks for a newer build and installs it in one click, or takes a .bin you downloaded from the releases page. Either way it writes a spare slot and rolls back if the new image fails to start.
A full flash from this page erases everything, including any rescue image you put in the device’s flash. That is fine for a first install; on a board you are only updating, the console route above keeps the rescue image (and your settings). Re-upload the rescue image afterwards if you use this page instead.
If the browser will not do it

Web Serial exists in Chrome and Edge on desktop, and nowhere else. Every other browser has to fall back to the command line, which does the same thing:

esptool --chip esp32p4 -b 921600 write-flash @flash_args

Take the full-flash archive from the releases page, unpack it, and run that inside the unpacked folder.

The installer on this page is esp-web-tools, bundled here rather than loaded from anywhere.

## What is an IP-KVM? Remote control of a computer from the BIOS up

Description: Remote desktop needs the computer to be working. An IP-KVM does not.

What is an IP-KVM? Remote control of a computer from the BIOS up

7 Sep 2026

explainer
hardware

An IP-KVM is a small box that gives you another computer's screen, keyboard and mouse over the network, in a browser. It plugs into the computer's video output and a USB port, so nothing has to be installed on the computer, and it keeps working when remote desktop cannot: in the BIOS, at a boot menu, on a machine that does not start, or with no operating system at all.

Most people know remote desktop. You sit at one computer and see the screen of another one. It is very useful. It also has one weak point: the far computer must be working. Its operating system must be running, and its network must be up.

When something goes wrong, that is exactly what is missing.

The computer stops at a black screen with a short message. It waits for someone to press a key. It shows the setup screen and stays there. The system does not start. The disk is empty and needs a new system. Or the computer is simply off. In all of these cases there is nothing running that remote desktop could talk to. So you get in a car, or you ask someone by phone to press buttons for you.

The idea

An IP-KVM solves this with hardware instead of software.

It is a small box. You plug it into the video output of the computer, and into one of its USB ports. That is all. Nothing is installed on the computer, and nothing has to be set up on it.

The computer now thinks that a screen and a keyboard are connected to it. It cannot tell that they are not real. The box takes the picture, sends it over the network, and you open it in a browser on your phone or laptop. What you type in that browser goes back to the computer as key presses.

A computer with a small box on its video and USB. The box sends the picture to a browser, and the keys come back the same way.

The name is old and not very friendly. KVM means keyboard, video, mouse - the three things such a box carries. IP means it does this over the network. So: keyboard, screen and mouse of one computer, over the network, in a browser.

It needs nothing from the operating system, and it does not care whether the computer runs Windows, Linux or nothing at all. It works while the computer is still starting up, which is where every other tool is blind.

Servers have had this for years

This is not a new idea. Real servers come with it built in. Different makers give it different names - iDRAC, iLO, IPMI - but the job is the same: reach the machine when its system is dead. People who work in data centres take it for granted.

Two things kept it out of normal life. It was built only into expensive server hardware, and the separate boxes that do the same for a normal computer cost several hundred euros or more.

That is the only thing that has changed. The idea is old. It is now cheap.

When it is useful

Here are the situations people actually describe.

Your parents live in another city, or another country. Their computer breaks now and then. Usually the fix is small - press a key, choose a different start option, undo a bad update. But over the phone it takes an hour, and sometimes it cannot be done at all. With a box on their computer, you open a browser and do it yourself in two minutes. They do not have to touch anything.

You at your computer, and the two of them at theirs. The same picture is on both screens, and you are the one pressing the keys.

You keep a computer at home that nobody sits at. A small server in a cupboard. A machine that stores films, or backups, or your photos. It has no screen and no keyboard, and it stands in a place that is hard to reach. It works for months, and then one day it does not answer. Without a screen you cannot even see why. This is the same box, on a shelf beside it.

A server on a shelf in a cupboard, with the box beside it, reached from a browser.

Your home is automated. The lights, the heating and the front door all go through one small computer. When it stops, the house stops with it, and that does not wait until you are home. If it will not start, there is nothing running on it to connect to - so the usual remote tools have nothing to talk to. The box does not need it to be running: it shows what the machine shows and types what you type, from the first second.

A house where the lights, the heating and the lock all run through one small computer, with the box beside it.

You need to install a system from far away. The box can also pretend to be a USB stick. A system image on its memory card is offered to the computer as if you had walked over and plugged one in, so a machine with an empty disk, in another building, can get a fresh system without anyone going there.

The card is written the ordinary way, in a card reader, before the box is left in place. One card holds several images, and the console picks which one the computer sees - so what it boots from can change later, even though the card cannot.

The disk images sit on the card inside the box. The one you pick is what the computer finds on its USB port.

The computer is switched off. A screen and a keyboard are of no use then. Two thin wires from the box to the power pins on the computer's board, and the button in the browser does what the button on the case does. Many computers can also be woken over the network, and the box can do that too.

Two thin wires from the box to the power pins on the board, and a power button in the browser.

You have a machine somewhere you cannot easily reach. A workshop. A summer house. A rented server in another country. An old computer that runs one program and must not be touched. The pattern is always the same: getting to it costs more than fixing it.

Two homes, far apart, with the box on the computer in the far one.
What it is not

It is not a replacement for remote desktop. When the far computer is healthy, remote desktop is faster and sharper, and it can move files. Use it.

An IP-KVM is for the other times, when there is nothing on the far machine left to connect to.

It does not carry sound, and it cannot repair broken hardware. It lets you see and press, exactly as if you were standing in front of the machine.

One warning

This box has full control of a computer. Anyone who reaches it can do anything to that machine. So do not put it directly on the internet.

Keep it on your home network and reach it through a VPN - a private tunnel to your own network. ESP-KVM has two built in, so this needs no extra equipment, and it takes about ten minutes to set up.

What it takes to build one

Two small boards, one flat cable, and no soldering. One board is the computer that does the work. The other turns the video signal into something it can read. You connect them, plug the pair into the machine you want to reach, and flash the firmware from a web page - there is nothing to install on your own computer either.

The quick start has the parts list and the steps. The whole thing is open source: you can read every line of it, change it, and build it yourself.

ESP-KVM is an open-source IP-KVM on the ESP32-P4 — the code is on GitHub, and you can install it from the browser or try the console without any hardware.
